## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nāmasiddhijātaka* (Ja 97) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection. The narrative was edited by V. Fausböll in the first volume of his edition of the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā* [Fausböll 1877].

The frame story is set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning a monk named Pāpaka ("Wicked") who held the superstitious belief that names possessed inherent power or determined luck and ill fortune, and who consequently wished to change his name [Shantibhikshu Sastri 1953; Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. The verse opens with the line *Jīvakañ ca mataṃ disvā* ("Seeing Quick [or Life] dead") [Fausböll 1877]. In the associated past narrative, a pupil unhappy with his name sets out to find a more auspicious one; along his journey, he encounters a deceased man named "Life" (Jīvaka), a beggar named "Wealthy", and a traveler named "Guide" who is hopelessly lost in the forest [Anandajoti 2010]. From these encounters he comes to the realization that a name is merely a designation without inherent significance or power [Shantibhikshu Sastri 1953; Anandajoti 2010].
